summary: Describes the VP8 compressed video data format and how to decode it. It is informational, so it documents the format rather than defining an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: VP8 is a way of squeezing video so it takes less space. This explains how the squeezed data is arranged and how a program can unsqueeze it into pictures.

what is the vp8 boolean entropy decoder
subtitle: How VP8 video is packed into bytes, and the exact steps a decoder follows to turn those bytes back into pictures.

tldr.problem: Raw video is huge, and different decoders must rebuild exactly the same pictures from the same compressed stream, or errors pile up from frame to frame.
tldr.mechanism: VP8 splits each frame into 16x16 macroblocks, predicts each one from earlier pixels (in the same frame or in earlier frames), adds a transformed and quantized correction, and codes everything with a probability-driven boolean entropy coder. The document gives the data layout and C code for each decoding step, using integer math only.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Informational document that describes the format and ships a reference decoder as its source-code attachment. Where the narrative and that code disagree, the code is correct.

today: RFC 6386 is an Informational, Independent Submission published in November 2011, and it is not on the Internet Standards Track. The RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment. No RFC in the metadata obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
RFC 6386 describes the VP8 compressed video data format together with the decoding procedure for it. It is meant to be used with the reference decoder source code in Attachment One (Section 20). If the narrative and the source code conflict, the reference source code is correct: the bitstream is defined by the code, not by the text.

Like many modern video schemes, VP8 breaks frames into square blocks of pixels, predicts each block from blocks already built, and adjusts the prediction with a discrete cosine transform (DCT). In one special case it uses a Walsh-Hadamard transform (WHT) instead. VP8 adds heavy use of contextual probabilities, which the RFC credits for a significant reduction in datarate at a given quality.

Unlike some older schemes such as the MPEG formats, VP8 specifies exact values for reconstructed pixels. The reconstruction algorithm uses fixed-precision integer operations only, so there is no "drift" from truncated fractions, and decoder correctness is easy to check. Postprocessing applied before display is outside the scope of the document and does not affect later frames.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the rulebook for unpacking VP8 video. The rules are so exact that every player must draw the very same picture, like everyone following the same recipe and getting the same cake.

sections.title: Pixels, Macroblocks and Frame Types
sections.content:
VP8 works only with 8-bit YUV 4:2:0 images. Each U or V (chroma) pixel lines up with a 2x2 block of Y (luma) pixels. Pixels are stored in raster order, left to right and top to bottom. A reserved bit in the header leaves room for a second color format.

Each frame is divided into macroblocks: 16x16 for Y and 8x8 for U and V. A macroblock is split into 4x4 subblocks, 16 for Y, 4 for U and 4 for V. The DCT always works on 4x4 blocks. A second-order block called Y2 holds the average intensities of the 16 Y subblocks and is coded with the WHT, so a macroblock has 24 real subblocks and sometimes a 25th virtual one.

There are only two frame types. Key frames (intraframes) decode without reference to any other frame and provide seeking points. Interframes are predicted from prior frames, up to and including the most recent key frame, so decoding is not tolerant of dropped frames. Unlike MPEG there is no bidirectional prediction. VP8 adds golden and altref frames as alternate references. Every key frame is automatically both, and an interframe may optionally replace either one. A typical use of golden frames is video conferencing, where re-sending a golden frame is cheaper than waiting for the next key frame.
sections.plainLanguage: A picture is cut into little squares, like a mosaic. Some pictures are drawn from scratch (key frames), and the others just say how they differ from earlier pictures, like a flip book that only redraws what moved.

sections.title: Frame Layout and the Decoding Process
sections.content:
Every compressed frame starts with an uncompressed data chunk: 10 bytes for key frames and 3 bytes for interframes. Then come two or more compressed partitions that begin and end on byte boundaries. The first holds the frame header and the per-macroblock prediction data. The rest hold the quantized DCT and WHT coefficients of the residue, which the RFC says typically accounts for roughly 70% of the datarate.

The coefficient data can be split across partitions by macroblock row. When there is more than one, the sizes of all but the last are written as 3-byte little-endian values right after the first partition, so a decoder can reach each one directly and work in parallel. Seeking inside a partition is not supported.

A decoder keeps four YUV frame buffers: the current frame, the previous frame, the golden frame and the altref frame. Buffers are padded with copies of edge pixels so predictions can reach outside the visible image. For each frame, the decoder reads the header, processes macroblocks in raster order (prediction data before residue), applies the loop filter to the whole frame, optionally replaces the golden or altref buffer, and swaps the current and last buffers. The RFC suggests getting key-frame-only streams working first, then adding interframes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame arrives as a little package: a short label, then a list of instructions, then the bits for fixing details. The player keeps a few older pictures nearby to copy from.

sections.title: The Boolean Entropy Decoder
sections.content:
Almost the entire VP8 stream is coded with a boolean entropy coder, a variant of an arithmetic coder. It encodes one yes/no value (a bool) at a time, using a probability that both sides know, so a bool that is very likely to be zero costs far less than one bit. The RFC notes that Huffman coding is just the special case where every probability is 128 (one half). Because most bools in VP8 are far from 50/50, this coder is critical to its performance.

Probabilities are 8-bit values, and the probability of a zero is p/256. The coder keeps a range that stays between 128 and 255 and computes split = 1 + (((range - 1) * probability) >> 8). The decoder starts with range = 255 and reads the first 2 bytes into its value. It returns a zero if the value is below the split, otherwise a one, then doubles the range until it is at least 128. The RFC gives full C code for the encoder and decoder.

On top of bools, VP8 builds literals L(n) (n flags read high to low), signed literals, optional values written F? X, and tree-coded values. A tree has the alphabet as leaves and a probability at each interior node. A tree for n values has n-1 interior nodes, and a value at depth x takes x bool reads. The largest tree, for DCT tokens, has 12 values. The RFC strongly suggests using its enumeration values and probability table layouts exactly.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine guessing a number with yes-or-no questions. If you already know the likely answer, you need fewer questions. The decoder uses the odds it is told about to read lots of answers from very few bits.

sections.title: The Frame Header
sections.content:
The 3-byte frame tag holds a 1-bit frame type (0 for key frames, 1 for interframes), a 3-bit version, a 1-bit show_frame flag and a 19-bit size of the first partition in bytes. Versions 0 to 3 are four profiles. Version 0 uses a bicubic reconstruction filter, versions 1 and 2 bilinear, and version 3 none. The RFC says that in decoding, the only loop filter settings that matter are those in the frame header.

Key frames add 7 more uncompressed bytes: the start code 0x9d 0x01 0x2a, then 16 bits each for width and height, where the top 2 bits of each is an upscaling code (0 none, 1 for 5/4, 2 for 5/3, 3 for 2) and the low 14 bits are the size. Upscaling does not affect the reconstruction buffer, which stays at the encoded size. When the size is not a multiple of 16, the extra columns and rows are decoded but discarded before output.

The first partition then carries the rest of the header: color space and clamping bits (key frames only), optional segment-based adjustments, loop filter type and levels, the number of coefficient partitions (1, 2, 4 or 8), six quantizer indices, golden and altref refresh flags, coefficient probability updates and the skip and mode probabilities. Probability tables persist across interframes and are reset to defaults on every key frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the cover page of each frame. It says how big the picture is, how to unpack it, and which older pictures to keep.

sections.title: Prediction, Coefficients and Reconstruction
sections.content:
For intra prediction, a luma macroblock uses one of four whole-block modes: DC_PRED, V_PRED, H_PRED and TM_PRED ("True Motion"). The fifth, B_PRED, lets each of the 16 Y subblocks pick one of 10 modes, adding six diagonal ones. Chroma uses the first four. Key-frame subblock modes are coded using the modes of the subblocks above and to the left as context. Predictions use reconstructed but not yet loop-filtered pixels. Pixels beyond the left edge are assumed to be 129 and those above the top edge 127.

The residue is coded as tokens from a 12-value alphabet: values 0 to 4, six category tokens for larger ranges (up to 2048), and an end-of-block token. After the tree-coded token, a sign flag follows for non-zero values. Probabilities come from a table indexed by plane type, coefficient band and a context of how busy the neighbors are. Macroblocks other than B_PRED and SPLITMV start with the Y2 block.

Each coefficient is then multiplied by one of six dequantization factors (looked up from the two tables in Section 14 using 7-bit indices), the Y2 block is inverted with the inverse WHT, the 24 subblocks are inverted with the inverse DCT, and the result is added to the prediction.
sections.plainLanguage: First the player guesses what a square looks like by copying from its neighbors. Then it adds a small correction to fix the guess, a bit like a teacher's red pen.

sections.title: Inter Prediction and Motion Vectors
sections.content:
In an interframe, each macroblock starts with a bool saying whether it is intra or inter predicted. An inter macroblock then selects a reference frame (previous, golden or altref) and a mode: mv_zero, mv_nearest, mv_near, mv_new or mv_split. Nearest and near vectors come from a survey of already-decoded vectors in up to 3 nearby macroblocks. SPLITMV divides the macroblock into two, four or sixteen pieces, each with its own vector.

A motion vector has a row and a column component, each a displacement in quarter pixels for luma that is coded with an absolute value and a sign. Components lie between -1023 and +1023. Values from 0 to 7 are tree-coded, larger ones are coded bit by bit. Chroma vectors are never sent. Each is the average of the vectors of the four luma subblocks covering the same area, giving 1/8-pixel resolution.

Whole-pixel vectors simply copy a block. Fractional ones are interpolated by two one-dimensional filters, reaching three pixels either side, and the version number picks bicubic or bilinear filtering. Encoders and decoders must keep motion vectors within -4096 to 4095 full pixels, and the maximum image size is 16383x16383.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of redrawing a ball, the video says "take the ball from the last picture and slide it a little to the right." That slide is a motion vector.

sections.title: The Loop Filter
sections.content:
After all macroblocks are rebuilt, a loop filter smooths the edges between macroblocks and between subblocks to reduce blocking artifacts. It is called a loop filter because it is inside the coding loop: its output is what later frames are predicted from. That makes it different from optional postprocessing, so a conformant decoder must apply it exactly as described.

There are two types, a cheaper simple filter and a normal filter. The frame header sets the type, a 6-bit loop_filter_level and a 3-bit sharpness_level. Deltas based on reference frame and prediction mode, and per-segment overrides, can adjust the level. If the level is 0 at either the frame or macroblock-override level, filtering must be skipped entirely, not run with a value of 0.
sections.plainLanguage: When you build with square blocks, you can see the seams. The loop filter is like lightly rubbing the seams so the picture looks smooth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC points to RFC 4732 and RFC 3552 and calls it extremely important that a decoder be robust against malicious payloads. Malicious data must not make the decoder overrun its allocated memory or consume inordinate resources. The same applies to an encoder, since misbehavior there might give an attacker access to transcoding gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could send a trick video made to crash the player. The player has to be built so that no sneaky file can break it.
